newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia reformers face battle with financial barons.
newsitem.headline: Russia reformers face battle with financial barons.

text.p: Liberal reformers in the Kremlin have emerged on top after a battle over two controversial state sell-offs, but the cost could be a long and bitter war with some of Russia's powerful financial barons.

A new determination to ensure open and fair auctions of stakes in state firms marks a watershed in privatisation, which until now has enabled state assets to pass into the hands of a few favoured groups at bargain basement prices.

It also signals a warning from the reformers, led by First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, to a group of financiers which bankrolled President Boris Yeltsin's re-election last year to expect no more favours from the Kremlin.
"Chubais wants to show that the Kremlin cannot be manipulated by financial structures any more," said Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation think-tank.
"He thinks they have got all their rewards for the election campaign, now it's over and it's time to cut them down to size."
The two auctions were won by the same bank, Uneximbank, to the wrath of business rivals who have hit back through the media empires they own.

"The victory of Uneximbank...will launch a new battle, possibly the fiercest and therefore the final one, between rival banking groups," said the daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta, controlled by the empire of tycoon-turned-politician Boris Berezovsky.

The daily Sevodnya, owned by banker and media magnate Vladimir Gusinsky, blazed: "The last 10 days have shaken Russia's political system and put in question the achievements of the economic reforms in recent years."

ZAO Svift, a firm representing Uneximbank, won a tender for a controlling stake in Norilsk Nickel metals group on Monday with a bid of $250 million. Uneximbank, which is headed by former government minister Vladimir Potanin, also led an international consortium that won a $1.875-billion, quarter stake in the Svyazinvest telecoms holding on July 25.
Gusinsky, Potanin and Berezovsky were part of the group of seven businessmen who met in the Swiss city of Davos and decided to get together to back Yeltsin's election campaign last year.

Since Yeltsin's victory last July, Berezovsky has been appointed to the influential post of secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council and Gusinsky's television network has won more air-time.
Potanin became a first deputy prime minister last August but lost his place in a reshuffle this spring.
The financiers' marriage of convenience has now broken down and Potanin's former allies look likely to combine forces to try to prevent him building too powerful an empire.

They say Uneximbank had an unfair advantage in the Norilsk Nickel tender and that it deprived Russia of potential revenues. They describe the Svyazinvest auction as a shadowy affair between state officials and financial magnates.
The business tycoons' influence had been under threat since young reformer Boris Nemtsov joined Chubais as a first deputy prime minister in the government reshuffle.
Nemtsov is a vocal supporter of open and fair sell-offs to provide funds to pay wage arrears to millions of workers.
"This time the president's team has shown publicly that from now on it considers itself free of any obligations to certain members of 'the Davos group'," the weekly Moscow News wrote.
"Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky think otherwise, as events have shown. They are ready to resist with all means available to them, including the mass media."
The Kremlin's ability to be independent of major financiers may prove limited, just as the bankers may be unwilling to go too far in distancing themselves from the Kremlin.
Both sides may need each other in the next presidential election, due in the year 2000, if they again feel a need to club together for what they see as a quest to protect reforms.
But that ability to cooperate may have been dented by the ill feeling created over Svyazinvest and Norilsk Nickel. Fierce media attacks on Nemtsov could cause particular problems.

Nemtsov is front-runner to become the Kremlin's candidate in the next presidential election but the chances of Berezovsky and Gusinsky backing him now appear slim. Their stakes in television channels and newspapers could be vital in an election campaign.

One alternative as the Kremlin's candidate remains stolid Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who sided against Potanin by trying to postpone the Norilsk Nickel tender and then calling for an investigation into the sale.
His failure to have the sale delayed was a setback to his own authority, but it may have pushed him closer to Berezovsky and Gusinsky and increased his chances of winning their backing.
